newsitem.title: USA: As US stocks adjust to "new" economy, bonds don't.
newsitem.headline: As US stocks adjust to "new" economy, bonds don't.

text.p: A healthy economy coupled with no signs of inflationary pressures, a Federal Reserve unlikley to ratchet interest rates up substantially and major progress on a balanced budget deal seems like a good recipe for both stocks and bonds.

But for more than a year, U.S. stock prices have soared while bond prices have struggled, leading many analysts to believe the stock market has adjusted to the "new" economy of solid growth, low unemployment, high productivity and low inflation while the bond market has not adjusted and is still living in the past.

"Bond people are having a difficult time believing we could have growth close to 3 percent and not have that translate into upward pressure on inflation," said Steven Slifer, chief economist at Lehman Brothers Inc.

Therefore the bond market remains constantly worried that the U.S economy's growth rate continues to average above three percent while its unemployment rate keeps falling -- hitting a 24-year low in April at 4.9 percent -- which will eventually lead to wage pressures leading bond prices to suffer heavily.

Wages have risen, but mainly in the high technology sector and in factories where the productivity gains have been greatest. Still, the market had been on alert for a rate hike since last July. Even though the Fed left rates alone at its May policy setting meeting, most traders and analysts believe the Fed still has a couple of more tightening steps to take.
The move to tighter monetary policy in March has clearly impacted both stocks and bonds, but in different ways.

Since the beginning of the year, June bond futures have fallen 3.4 percent and the U.S. Treasury 30-year bond's yield rose to 7 percent from a low of 6.64 percent on December 31, while June stock futures have risen 13.3 percent and the Dow Jones industrial average has jumped nearly 1,000 points as it flirts with record levels almost daily evaporating a 10 percent correction in stocks and putting the Dow in sight of the 8,000 point level by year's end.

Much of the stock market's success stems from corporate earnings that surpassed analysts expectations. But, analysts noted, the good earnings result from increased worker productivity and companies operating more efficiently.

"Companies are keeping a tight reign on margins, so at the first hint of earnings slipping, they lay off people," said Slifer. "Firms are paying close attention to labor costs but the bond market hasn't figured that out yet and continues to worry about wage pressures."

Consumer inflation has stuck close to a 3 percent rate the past five years and is running at a 2.5 percent pace in 1997. But U.S. Treasury bond yields are about 7 percent. That 450 basis points spread is well above the historical norm of a 250 basis points between inflation and bonds.
So, bond yields should be at 5 percent given the current environment and historical patterns, analysts said.
"It's not (actual) inflation but the risk" spooking the bond market, said Allen Sinai, chief global economist at Primark Descision Economics. "I think the pricing is about right."
Sinai argued that in the past, a strong economy and a tight labor market led to a pickup in inflation.

This time around "we won't get history, but the bond market can't forget history -- and shouldn't," he said. "Someday, it will become crystal clear that the new economy will persist. Then, we will have a big rally in bonds. But for now, it is more likely (bonds) will have more trouble before the way is clear."
Numerous factors point in favor of stocks outperforming bonds in the near term, Peter Canello, chief U.S. investment strategist at Dean Witter Reynolds said.
"Everything I can think of helps the stock market and nothing helps the bond market," Canello said.

He cited favorable valuations and a slim 5 percent spread between stocks and bonds as a key reason more money is flowing into stocks, as well as the strong corporate earnings, a strong economy, a likely capital gains tax cut and huge stock inflows from 401(K) plans.
Allocations for equities are generally stronger than for bonds from 401(K)'s by a 75 percent to 25 percent ratio. This ratio could widen as more people realize they are underinvensted for retirement.

At the same time, the U.S. budget deal favors stocks over bonds since the first few years of the five-year accord to balance the budget will have tax cuts and spending increases, only to reverse after the year 2000, some analysts argued.
Analysts also pointed out that the bond market doesn't usually like a strong economy because of its inflation potential, while a healthy economy is typically good for earnings.
Furthermore current monetary policy helps stock prices as a few small rate hikes should ensure a longer non-inflationary economic expansion.
"Stocks are winning because in a strong economy, good profits beat out (rising) interest rates," said Bob DiClemente, senior economist at Salomon Brothers.

"But it could be worse for bonds," he added. "We may not be at 6.5 percent (on bonds) but we are not at 7.5 percent either. The last time we were at 5.5 percent (fed funds), we were at least 50 basis points higher (for the long bond)."

Indeed, when the Fed hiked rates by 75 basis points to 5.5 percent on November 15, 1994, the 30-year bond yield was above 8 percent. The stock market also performed rather poorly for much of 1994 as interest rates rose significantly.

"Inflation has stopped falling and slack has eroded. So, if demand continues the way it has the past year then there will be further real rate pressures and further challenges to the stock market," said DiClemente. "We'll get higher rates and a squeeze on profit margins, which could be a tough go on equites."

"There is a limit to how much of a different direction the equity market could go given current circumstances," said Bruce Steinberg, chief economist at Merrill Lynch & Co. "Bond yields over 7 percent will have an impact on equities in the near term."
(( -- N.A. Treasury Desk, 212-859-1867 ))
